2027-04-25.title: Fifth Sunday of Easter
readings: Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles
I will praise you, Lord, in the assembly of your people (or: Alleluia)
Let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action
I am the vine, you are the branches
2027-04-25.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. The feast of St Mark the Evangelist (25 April) is not celebrated this year, because a Sunday of Easter takes precedence over a feast; it is not transferred. Regina Caeli at noon until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-25.verse: I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
theo: The first reading shows us Saul of Tarsus after his conversion, trying to join the disciples in Jerusalem. It does not go well. “They were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple.” And who could blame them? Only a short time before he had been dragging Christians to prison. Saul has met the risen Lord, but the Church does not yet trust him. Then one man changes everything: “Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles, and described for them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.” Barnabas, the “son of encouragement,” takes a risk on a man everyone else feared. Without Barnabas, perhaps there would have been no St Paul as we know him. Soon Saul is preaching boldly in Jerusalem, his life is threatened again, and the believers send him off to Tarsus to keep him safe. Luke ends with a beautiful summary: “the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace and was built up. Living in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it increased in numbers.”

The Psalm is the second half of Psalm 22, the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” On Palm Sunday of the Passion we sang from its first half, the cry of anguish. In the Easter season the Church sings its second half, the song of thanksgiving of one who has been rescued: “From you comes my praise in the great congregation.” “The poor shall eat and be satisfied.” “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.” The one who was forsaken now praises God in the assembly, and his deliverance will be told “to a people yet unborn.” That is the Resurrection, and that is the Church, the great congregation where the risen Christ praises the Father with us.

The second reading, from the First Letter of John, is short and very practical: “Little children, let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action.” Christian love is not a feeling or a speech; it is shown in deeds. Then John speaks tenderly to troubled consciences: “whenever our hearts condemn us; for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.” When we feel unworthy, our feelings do not have the last word; God does. And he sums up the whole of Christian life in one commandment with two parts: “that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another.” Faith and love are not two separate things; they are one life. “All who obey his commandments abide in him, and he abides in them. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit that he has given us.”

The Gospel gives us one of the richest images of the whole Bible. At the Last Supper Jesus says: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinegrower.” In the Old Testament Israel was God's vine, planted with love and tended with care (Isaiah 5; Psalm 80). Now Jesus says that he himself is the true vine, and we are the branches. The life of the branch is the life of the vine; cut off, it withers. “Abide in me as I abide in you.” The word “abide” appears again and again: to stay, to remain, to make one's home. And the Father prunes: “Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.” Pruning hurts, but it is not punishment; it is the vinegrower's care, so that the branch may bear more. “Apart from me you can do nothing.” We cannot love as 1 John asks by our own effort; we can only love if the life of Christ flows in us. The Barnabas of the first reading is such a branch: his encouragement of Paul was the fruit of Christ's own life in him. Today would ordinarily be the feast of St Mark the Evangelist, the same John Mark who was Barnabas's cousin. This year the Sunday takes its place, but we may thank God for him, who wrote the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, so that it could bear fruit in every age.
conn: Paul himself says he went up to Jerusalem three years after his conversion to visit Cephas, and stayed with him fifteen days (Galatians 1:18). Luke tells the story more briefly and from the Church's side.
A Levite from Cyprus, the “son of encouragement” (Acts 4:36). His trust in Paul is the first of many times he stands up for someone others have rejected (see Acts 15:37–39, with John Mark).
Here Greek-speaking Jews in Jerusalem, perhaps the same synagogue circles that had argued with Stephen (Acts 6:9). Paul now stands where Stephen stood.
Paul's home city in Cilicia, in south-eastern Asia Minor, a centre of learning. He will remain there until Barnabas comes to fetch him for Antioch (Acts 11:25).

The psalm whose first verse Jesus cried out on the cross (Mark 15:34). Its second half moves from lament to praise and to a vision of all nations worshipping God. The early Church saw in it the whole paschal mystery.
The Greek menein appears seven times in John 15:4–7. It means to stay, to remain, to dwell. The same word is used when the first disciples “remained” with Jesus (John 1:39).
Israel is God's vine in Isaiah 5:1–7, Jeremiah 2:21, Psalm 80:8–16 and Hosea 10:1. A great golden vine decorated the entrance to the Temple sanctuary in Jesus' day.
In Greek the word for “prunes” (kathairei) is close to the word for “cleansed” (katharoi) in verse 3. The word of Jesus is the knife that cleanses and prunes.
In the Table of Liturgical Days the Sundays of Easter rank above feasts of the Lord's apostles and evangelists. A feast impeded by a Sunday is simply omitted that year.
altar: “I am the vine, you are the branches.” At the Last Supper, where Jesus spoke these words, he took the cup of “the fruit of the vine” and made it his Blood. In Holy Communion the life of the Vine flows into the branches.

The Second Vatican Council calls the Eucharist the source and summit of the Christian life. To abide in Christ is, above all, to abide in his Eucharist: “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them” (John 6:56).
outline: Show a cut branch from a garden: green today, dry in three days. Ask: what keeps me green?
Point 2 · Not in word, but in truth and action
Love that is shown, and the God who is greater than our hearts.
Point 4 · Pruned to bear more fruit
Suffering in the hands of the vinegrower.
A vineyard in harvest, the branches bent low with grapes, and the vinegrower smiling among them.
“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
live: Find one person in your parish or family who is distrusted or left out. Speak up for them, introduce them, or simply sit with them.
Choose one act of love this week that costs you something: visit, phone, help, pay a bill, forgive. Do it without announcing it.
Make one daily habit of abiding: a short visit to the Blessed Sacrament, the Rosary, or ten minutes with the Gospel. A branch needs the vine every day, not only on Sundays.
Bring to the Father one painful loss or limitation in your life, and pray: Prune me, Lord, so that I may bear more fruit.
fathers: The branches are in the vine in such a way that they give nothing to the vine but receive their life from it. One of two things belongs to the branch: either the vine or the fire. If it is not in the vine, it will be in the fire; let it be in the vine, that it may not be in the fire.

Love, and do what you will. If you keep silence, keep silence out of love; if you cry out, cry out out of love; if you correct, correct out of love; if you spare, spare out of love. Let the root of love be within, for from that root nothing but good can grow.

Barnabas was a true son of encouragement: he did not let the past of Paul stand between Paul and the Church, but took him by the hand and led him to the apostles. So should we do for those who have turned to God.
Christ is the vine; we are joined to him by the Holy Spirit and nourished by his flesh, so that his very life becomes ours.
magis: The Church is a cultivated field, the vineyard of God; Christ is the true vine who gives life and fruitfulness to the branches.
The Church is communion with Jesus: “Abide in me, and I in you.” The Church is the Body of Christ.
“Apart from me you can do nothing”: the fruit of the Christian life comes from union with Christ.
The Holy Spirit unites the Church to the life and mission of Christ; the fruit of the Spirit in the liturgy is communion.
The liturgy, and above all the Eucharist, is the source and summit of the Church's life.
Love of God and love of neighbour are inseparable: love grows through love, in action.
saints: St Mark the Evangelist (not kept this year)

John Mark, cousin of Barnabas, companion of Paul and of Peter, whom tradition names as the author of the Gospel according to Mark and the founder of the Church of Alexandria. His symbol is the lion. His feast is omitted in 2027 because 25 April is the Fifth Sunday of Easter.

26–30 Apr: Fifth Week of Easter. 28 Apr: St Peter Chanel; St Louis Grignion de Montfort (optional). 29 Apr: St Catherine of Siena (memorial). 30 Apr: St Pius V (optional). 1 May: St Joseph the Worker (optional); May, the month of the Blessed Virgin Mary, begins.
2027-04-25.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, true vine, your Father is the vinegrower and we are the branches. Keep us abiding in you, for apart from you we can do nothing. Nourish us with your word and with your Body and Blood, so that your life may flow in us and bear fruit that lasts. When the Father prunes us, give us trust in his loving hands. Make us like Barnabas, quick to welcome and to encourage; teach us to love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action; and when our hearts condemn us, remind us that God is greater than our hearts. With St Mark, who wrote your Gospel, and with the Blessed Virgin Mary, the fruitful branch who bore you, we praise you in the assembly of your people, now and for ever. Alleluia. Amen.

quick: Barnabas brought Saul, whom all feared, to the apostles; the Church grew in peace and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.
Let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action; God is greater than our hearts.
Jesus: I am the vine, you are the branches; abide in me; apart from me you can do nothing.
2027-04-25.action: Do one costly act of love this week, quietly, as fruit of the Vine.
2027-04-25.question: Where in my life am I trying to bear fruit without abiding in Jesus?
catechism: Communion with Jesus: abide in me.
Apart from me you can do nothing.
kidsaint: Mark was a young helper of St Paul and St Peter. Once he got scared and went home, but later he came back and became a great helper. He wrote down the story of Jesus in the Gospel of Mark, the shortest Gospel, full of action! His symbol is a lion. Lesson: even if we get scared or make mistakes, Jesus can still use us to do great things.
2027-04-25.special: Fifth Sunday of Easter, Year B: Gloria and Creed; the feast of St Mark is omitted this year; Regina Caeli at noon.
term: To remain, stay, dwell (Greek menein). In John's Gospel and letters it describes the lasting union of the disciple with Christ, through faith, love, the word and the Eucharist. To abide is not to visit Jesus sometimes but to live in him.

family.explain: Jesus says: I am the vine, a grape plant, and you are the branches. A branch that stays joined to the plant gets everything it needs and grows lots of grapes. But a branch that is broken off dries up. If we stay close to Jesus, by praying, going to Mass and loving others, his life flows into us, and we do good things.
family.intention: We pray for anyone in our family or among our friends who has drifted away from Jesus, that they may come back and be joined to the Vine again.
family.ask: Ask: “What helps our family stay joined to Jesus?” Choose one thing to do together every day this week, such as night prayer, and keep it faithfully.

illus: In a parish near Kochi, a man released from prison after many years began coming to the early Sunday Mass. People moved away from him in the pew. The parish's St Vincent de Paul conference president, a retired bank clerk, noticed. The next Sunday he sat next to the man, invited him for tea, and later found him work at a friend's printing press. When some parishioners complained, he said quietly: Barnabas did this for Paul. Two years later the same man was serving as a volunteer in the parish kitchen for the poor, and people who once avoided him now ask for him by name.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, true vine, we are your branches. Keep us in you, and let your life flow in us so that we bear much fruit. Alleluia. Amen.
share: Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles (Acts 9:27). Who needs me to stand by them as Barnabas stood by Paul?
Let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action (1 John 3:18). What act of love have I been only talking about?
Apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). Where am I trying to manage without Jesus?
pm.resp: I will praise you, Lord, in the assembly of your people.
interc: For the Church, that she may live in peace, be built up and grow in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.
For those who are distrusted because of their past, that they may find a Barnabas in our community.
For those whose hearts condemn them, that they may know that God is greater than their hearts.
For all who are being pruned by suffering, illness or loss, that they may bear more fruit.
For our group, that we may abide in Christ every day and love in truth and action.
pm.close: Father, vinegrower of the vineyard of your Church, keep us joined to Christ the true vine, and make us bear fruit that gives you glory. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, if you cut a branch from a mango tree, for a day or two it stays green. It looks alive. But it has no future. In a few days its leaves are dry. Jesus says today: I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5).

Look at the first reading. Saul, the former persecutor, comes to Jerusalem, but everyone is afraid of him. Nobody trusts him. Then Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles (Acts 9:27). Barnabas trusted when others feared. He gave Paul a place in the Church.

Where did Barnabas get that courage and that generosity? From the Vine. He was a branch joined to Christ, and the fruit of Christ's life in him was encouragement. Is there someone in our parish, perhaps someone with a bad past, a broken family, a different background, who needs a Barnabas? Will you be that person?

St John tells us in the second reading: little children, let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action (1 John 3:18). Our love must be seen. And if our hearts accuse us, if we feel we are not good enough, John says: God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything. Do not let guilt cut you off from the Vine; bring it to him in confession.

Jesus also speaks of pruning. The Father prunes every fruitful branch to make it bear more fruit. Sometimes life cuts us: illness, loss, failure. It hurts. But in the Father's hands, pruning is not punishment; it is love preparing a greater harvest.

How do we abide in Christ? In prayer every day. In the word of God. Above all in the Eucharist: whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. Today is also the day we would have kept the feast of St Mark, who wrote the Gospel. Let us thank God for him, and for the Blessed Virgin Mary, whose month begins this week. Let us stay joined to the Vine, and bear much fruit. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, a branch on a plant gets its food from the plant. If you break it off, it dries up. Jesus says: I am the vine, you are the branches!
When we pray, go to Mass and love others, we stay joined to Jesus, and we grow good fruit like kindness and joy. Let us say: Jesus, keep me close to you!

intro: Theme: “I am the vine, you are the branches.”
Barnabas who welcomed Saul, love in truth and action, abiding in Christ, and the Father's pruning.

sub: The Church at peace and growing.
q: You shall also love the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.
But Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles, and described for them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.
points.apply: This week, stand beside one person whom others distrust or avoid.

q: For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.
Little children, let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action.
points.apply: Turn one good intention you have been talking about into a deed before next Sunday.

sub: The vine of Israel and the true vine.
The life of the branch is the life of the vine.
q: Let me sing for my beloved my love-song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill.
I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
points.apply: Choose a daily way of abiding: a visit to the Blessed Sacrament, the Rosary or ten minutes with the Gospel, and keep it all week.

sub: Glory to the Father in much fruit.
q: You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.
He removes every branch in me that bears no fruit. Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.
points.apply: Offer to the Father one painful situation in your life, asking him to make it fruitful.

concl: Christ is the true vine; joined to him by faith, the word and the Eucharist, we live with his life.
The fruit of abiding in him is love in truth and action, like the welcome Barnabas gave to Paul.
2027-04-25.resolve: Abide with Jesus every day this week, and let one act of love be its fruit.
